exam: Icewine: natural freezing on the vine, picking at minus 8°C or colder, pressing while frozen, at least 35 Brix at the press, and no freezing of picked grapes.
Vidal Blanc, a hybrid, makes most icewine; Riesling and Cabernet Franc follow.
The two regions: the Niagara Peninsula beside Lake Ontario under the escarpment, and the Okanagan Valley in British Columbia, irrigated and close to desert in the south.
VQA: a provincial system, run by VQA Ontario and the BC Wine Authority, guaranteeing origin, variety and a tasting panel; an international blend sits outside it.

Niagara's structure: ten sub-appellations and, as reviewed in October 2026, three regional appellations: Niagara-on-the-Lake, Niagara Escarpment and West Niagara. Ontario's other main appellations are Lake Erie North Shore and Prince Edward County.
The southern Okanagan: Golden Mile Bench, the first sub-appellation in 2015, facing Black Sage Bench across the valley.
Inniskillin: founded in 1975, and its 1989 Vidal Icewine won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in 1991.

grapes.name: Vidal Blanc
grapes.styles: The thick skinned hybrid behind most Canadian icewine, hanging intact on the vine into deep winter and giving tropical fruit, apricot and bright acidity.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Niagara's finest white, dry to off dry from the benches, with lime and stone and a long life, and the second icewine grape.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Cool climate Chardonnay of real tension from the Niagara benches, Prince Edward County and the Okanagan, oaked or not, and the base of much sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Ontario's red success, ripening where Cabernet Sauvignon struggles, with raspberry and leafy lift; also a pink, berry scented icewine.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Fine boned and red fruited in Prince Edward County and on the Niagara benches, fuller in the Okanagan.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: British Columbia's leading red, ripe and plush from the southern Okanagan, alone or in Bordeaux style blends.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: The Okanagan's leading white, ripe and pear scented, often with a touch of sweetness.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripe only on the warmest sites, the southern Okanagan above all, and usually blended with Merlot and Cabernet Franc.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Dark, peppery Syrah from the hot southern Okanagan and the Similkameen.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: Bright, juicy, red fruited reds in Niagara, a growing cool climate style.

grapes.name: Baco Noir
grapes.styles: A French bred hybrid red long grown in Ontario, dark, sharp and smoky, kept by loyal drinkers.

grapes.name: L'Acadie Blanc
grapes.styles: A cold hardy hybrid bred in Ontario and adopted by Nova Scotia, crisp and citrus, the signature grape of Tidal Bay.

labels: written as one word on a Canadian label: sweet wine from grapes frozen naturally on the vine, picked at minus 8°C or colder, pressed frozen, at least 35 Brix
icewine with a sparkle, a Niagara speciality
Late Harvest, Select Late Harvest, Special Select Late Harvest
the late picked sweet wines below icewine, rising in sugar at harvest
Ontario's term for a sweet wine from nobly rotten, shrivelled berries
Vintners Quality Alliance, the provincial appellation and standards system
Nova Scotia's appellation for a crisp, dry or off dry white from local grapes, with L'Acadie Blanc the signature among them
Quebec's protected indication for wine grown and made in the province
ladder: VQA, provincial designation
Ontario or British Columbia on a VQA label: every grape grown in that province, laboratory analysis, and a tasting panel before the wine may carry the VQA mark.
VQA, viticultural area

Ontario's Designated Viticultural Areas (Niagara Peninsula, Lake Erie North Shore, Prince Edward County) and British Columbia's geographical indications (Okanagan Valley, Similkameen Valley, Fraser Valley, Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands and newer interior names): the great majority of the fruit from the area named.
Sub-appellation

As reviewed in October 2026, the Niagara Peninsula has ten sub-appellations and three regional appellations: Niagara-on-the-Lake, Niagara Escarpment and West Niagara. West Niagara covers the six sub-appellations west of the Welland Canal. British Columbia has its own sub-GIs, including Golden Mile Bench, Okanagan Falls, Naramata Bench and Skaha Bench.
Single vineyard
A named vineyard inside an appellation, with all the fruit from that vineyard.
International blend

Wine bottled in Canada that blends imported bulk wine with Canadian wine: outside VQA, and labelled as an international blend from imported and domestic wines, the order of the words following which share is larger.
Provincial schemes outside VQA
Nova Scotia's Tidal Bay appellation for a crisp white, and Quebec's protected indication Vin du Québec, each under its own provincial rules.
canada.overview:
Wine came late and hard. Native and hybrid grapes, labrusca above all, served a market for sweet and fortified wine through most of the twentieth century, and Ontario's long hangover from Prohibition meant that no new winery licence was issued there between 1929 and 1975, when Inniskillin received one. Two shocks changed everything at the end of the 1980s. Free trade with the United States exposed growers to Californian wine, and British Columbia answered in 1988 by paying its growers to pull out most of their vineyard, which went back in as vinifera on the warmest sites. Ontario launched VQA as a voluntary standard the same year and wrote it into provincial law in 1999. In 1991 Inniskillin's 1989 Vidal Icewine won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in Bordeaux, and the world took notice.

Water makes the vineyards possible. Lake Ontario stores summer heat and gives it back slowly; its breezes strike the escarpment and roll back over the vines, holding budburst back until the danger of spring frost has passed and stretching the autumn. Lake Erie does the same, more warmly, for the Lake Erie North Shore and for Pelee Island, the country's southernmost vineyards. The Okanagan is different in kind: a glacial trench in the rain shadow of the coastal ranges, irrigated throughout, hot by day and cool by night, with long summer daylight close to fifty degrees north. In both places winter cold, not summer heat, sets the limit, and one hard freeze can kill buds or whole vines.

VQA belongs to the provinces. VQA Ontario and the BC Wine Authority keep separate rules, and the smaller provinces have arrangements of their own. A provincial name on a VQA label means every grape came from that province; a named area means the great majority did; a named variety must make up at least 85 per cent of the wine. Bottles that blend imported bulk wine with Canadian wine sit outside VQA altogether and must call themselves an international blend from imported and domestic wines; the old wording, Cellared in Canada, has been retired.

The exam leans on icewine above all: the minus 8°C rule, the 35 Brix floor at the press, natural freezing only and Vidal's thick skin. Then come the two regions and what each grows, what VQA guarantees, and a handful of names: Niagara-on-the-Lake and the Niagara Escarpment benches, Prince Edward County, and the Golden Mile and Black Sage benches of the southern Okanagan.

places.name: Ontario
places.note: The larger producer, with three viticultural areas strung along the shores of Lake Ontario and Lake Erie, where the lakes temper a hard continental winter; home of most Canadian icewine.

places.name: Niagara Peninsula
places.note: Ontario's largest appellation, most of it on the strip of land between Lake Ontario and the Niagara Escarpment, warmed in autumn and cooled in spring by the lake. Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir and Vidal lead, and most of the country's icewine is made here. Inniskillin at Niagara-on-the-Lake and Tawse on the Twenty Mile Bench are names to know.

places.name: Niagara-on-the-Lake
places.note: The regional appellation on the flat, warmer plain beside the lake and the Niagara River, home of Inniskillin and of much of the icewine harvest; St. David's Bench, Four Mile Creek, Niagara River and Niagara Lakeshore are its sub-appellations.

places.name: Niagara Escarpment
places.note: The regional appellation along the benches below the cliff, cooler and steeper, on clay rich in limestone, where lake breezes circulate against the slope: Beamsville Bench, Twenty Mile Bench and Short Hills Bench, prized for Riesling and Chardonnay.

places.name: Twenty Mile Bench
places.note: Rolling slopes under the escarpment near Jordan and Vineland, among Ontario's most admired sites for mineral Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; Tawse farms here.

places.name: Beamsville Bench
places.note: The westernmost of the three escarpment benches, a narrow shelf of clay over limestone close under the cliff, known for long lived Riesling and Chardonnay.

places.name: West Niagara
places.note: Regional appellation encompassing the six Niagara Peninsula sub-appellations west of the Welland Canal. It overlaps the more specific Niagara Escarpment regional appellation; these are not three mutually exclusive districts.

places.name: Lake Erie North Shore
places.note: Ontario's south western appellation on the north shore of Lake Erie, the warmest of the three, where shallow water lengthens the season; Pelee Island, out in the lake, holds the country's southernmost vineyards.

places.name: Prince Edward County
places.note: A limestone island on Lake Ontario's north eastern shore, so cold in winter that growers bury the vines under soil every November and uncover them in spring; Pinot Noir and Chardonnay of real tension from thin soils over limestone.

places.name: British Columbia
places.note: The western province, its vineyards in the dry interior valleys behind the coastal mountains and, on a smaller scale, on the wetter coast and islands around Vancouver.

places.name: Okanagan Valley
places.note: British Columbia's heart, a chain of deep lakes running north to south for more than two hundred kilometres: cooler and aromatic in the north around Kelowna, hot and close to desert in the south around Oliver and Osoyoos. Everything is irrigated. Merlot, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and the Bordeaux reds lead, and Mission Hill is the house to know.

places.name: Golden Mile Bench
places.note: The first sub-appellation in the Okanagan, on the valley's western side just south of Oliver: an east facing alluvial fan that warms early and falls into shade through the hot afternoon.

places.name: Black Sage Bench
places.note: The eastern side of the valley south of Oliver, deep windblown sand facing the afternoon sun, giving some of Canada's ripest Bordeaux reds and Syrah, often from vines on their own roots.

places.name: Naramata Bench and Skaha Bench
places.note: Lakeside slopes north and south of Penticton, recognised as sub-appellations in 2019, a year after Okanagan Falls, for Pinot Noir, Merlot and aromatic whites.

places.name: Similkameen Valley
places.note: The narrow, windy, rocky valley over the ridge west of the southern Okanagan, hot and dry, for Bordeaux reds and Syrah.

places.name: Coastal British Columbia
places.note: Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands and the Fraser Valley near Vancouver: maritime, wetter and cooler, with Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Ortega and sparkling wine.

places.name: Nova Scotia
places.note: Atlantic Canada's wine province, in the Annapolis and Gaspereau valleys beside the Bay of Fundy, cold and late. Tidal Bay is its appellation for a still, crisp white, with L'Acadie Blanc its signature grape, and Benjamin Bridge its traditional method sparkling estate.

places.name: Quebec
places.note: Vineyards south of Montreal and in the Eastern Townships on cold hardy hybrids and, increasingly, vinifera under winter covers, with its own indication, Vin du Québec, and ice cider, an invention of the province.

traps: Canada asks minus 8°C for icewine; Germany's figure for Eiswein, minus 7°C, comes from its courts and wine institute rather than the text of its wine law. The numbers are swapped on exams.
Freezing picked grapes in a freezer, cryoextraction, is barred: the frost must come on the vine.
Icewine carries no botrytis: pure fruit and acid, not honeyed rot. A nobly rotten Ontario wine is labelled Totally Botrytis Affected.
The Okanagan is not wet Pacific country: it lies in a rain shadow, is irrigated throughout and is close to desert at Osoyoos.
VQA is not federal. Each province writes its own rules, and Ontario's and British Columbia's thresholds differ.
Cellared in Canada is retired wording; imported blends now say international blend from imported and domestic wines, and they are never VQA.
Niagara Escarpment names an Ontario regional appellation and also a New York AVA across the river; read the country on the label.
The two regions are often called four thousand kilometres apart; that is nearer the distance by road. In a straight line it is a little over three thousand.

exam: Georgia first: the qvevri, the Kakhetian skin and stem method, Saperavi and Rkatsiteli, the Kakheti appellations by style, the 2013 UNESCO listing and the claim of 8,000 vintages.
Slovenia as Friuli's twin: Brda and Collio, Rebula and Ribolla Gialla, the three regions and their rivers, Cviček and Teran as traditional names.
Croatia: Plavac Mali and Dingač, Tribidrag as Zinfandel's identity, Malvazija Istarska, Graševina as Welschriesling, Pošip on Korčula.
Romania's Fetească trio, Dealu Mare, Cotnari and its Grasă, and the DOC suffixes CMD, CT and CIB.
Bulgaria's Mavrud, Melnik and Rubin, the two PGI zones and the Balkan range between them; Moldova's three regions and Purcari.
Czechia and Slovakia: Morava and Čechy, the ripeness ladder in Czech and Slovak words, VOC Znojmo, and Slovakia's seven Tokaj villages.
Grape synonyms across the borders: Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch as Frankovka and Modra frankinja, Furmint as Šipon, Kadarka as Gamza, Refošk as Teran.

grapes.name: Saperavi
grapes.styles: Georgia's great red, a teinturier with red flesh: deep colour, firm tannin and acidity, dry in Mukuzani and Napareuli, naturally semi-sweet in Kindzmarauli and Akhasheni, and travelled to Moldova.

grapes.name: Rkatsiteli
grapes.styles: The white workhorse of Kakheti, red stemmed and high in acid: crisp European style whites, or amber wine after months on skins in qvevri; Tsinandali's base.

grapes.name: Mtsvane
grapes.styles: Kakhetian green grape of aroma and softness, blended with Rkatsiteli in Tsinandali and alone in Manavi.

grapes.name: Plavac Mali
grapes.styles: Dalmatia's red, a cross of Tribidrag and Dobričić: dark, warm, high in alcohol and tannin, dried fig and carob, at its grandest on the Dingač and Postup slopes of Pelješac.

grapes.name: Tribidrag
grapes.styles: The Dalmatian vine also called Crljenak Kaštelanski, matched by DNA to Zinfandel, and so to Primitivo, in 2001 under that second name; nearly extinct at home, now replanted in small quantity.

grapes.name: Malvazija Istarska
grapes.styles: Istria's white: dry, full, with acacia, apricot and a bitter almond finish, fresh from steel or fuller after skin contact and acacia wood.

grapes.name: Pošip
grapes.styles: Korčula's white, full bodied and dry with ripe pear and almond; the best known of the Dalmatian island whites.

grapes.name: Graševina
grapes.styles: Welschriesling under its Croatian name, the country's most planted grape: crisp, dry, apple and bitter almond in Slavonia, late harvest and ice wine at Kutjevo in cold years.

grapes.name: Rebula
grapes.styles: Ribolla Gialla in Slovenian: fresh, lean and citric when made simply in Goriška Brda, textured and amber after long skin maceration.

grapes.name: Refošk
grapes.styles: Refosco: tart, dark and iron edged on the Kras, where it is sold as Teran, and in Slovenian and Croatian Istria.

grapes.name: Fetească Neagră
grapes.styles: Romania's native red, the black maiden: dark fruit, dried plum and spice with ripe tannin, best in Dealu Mare, often oaked, also in Moldova.

grapes.name: Fetească Regală
grapes.styles: The royal maiden, a Transylvanian natural cross found in the 1920s and among Romania's most planted whites: floral, fresh, dry, and a sparkling base.

grapes.name: Fetească Albă
grapes.styles: The white maiden, older and softer than Regală, with apricot and a light honeyed note; part of the Cotnari blend.

grapes.name: Grasă de Cotnari
grapes.styles: The fat grape of Cotnari, Hungary's Kövérszőlő, prone to botrytis and the heart of Cotnari's sweet wine.

grapes.name: Mavrud
grapes.styles: Bulgaria's late ripening native red around Asenovgrad and Plovdiv: dense, dark, tannic, with mulberry and spice, built for oak.

grapes.name: Rara Neagră
grapes.styles: Moldova's native red, Romania's Băbească Neagră: light in colour and body, fresh and red fruited, a partner to Cabernet and Saperavi in Negru de Purcari.

grapes.name: Pálava
grapes.styles: A Czech cross of Müller-Thurgau and Gewürztraminer bred in 1953: aromatic, rose and spice, often off dry, a Mikulov speciality.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.styles: Veltlínské zelené in Czech, Veltlínske zelené in Slovak: the leading white of Morava and the Small Carpathians, peppery and dry as in Austria.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.styles: Frankovka in Croatia, Czechia and Slovakia, Modra frankinja in Slovenia: the central European red of sour cherry and pepper, light to medium in these cool regions.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.styles: Šipon in Slovenia's Štajerska, where it makes dry, taut whites, and the base of the sweet wines of Slovak Tokaj.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The international red of Bulgaria, Romania and Moldova, planted at scale under socialism and now the backbone of estate reds in Dealu Mare, Thrace and Ștefan Vodă.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Bulgaria's and Romania's softening partner to Cabernet, and a Brda red in Slovenia beside the whites.

labels: the buried Georgian clay vessel; also spelt kvevri
a Georgian wine cellar, often a row of buried qvevri
a Georgian legal style, the sweetness left by a fermentation stopped by cold, as in Kindzmarauli
Croatian for red (literally black), white and rosé; suho is dry, slatko sweet
Dalmatian sweet wine from dried grapes, still and often amber
Slovenian for red and white; suho dry, polsuho off dry, sladko sweet
pozna trgatev, izbor, jagodni izbor, suhi jagodni izbor, ledeno vino
the Slovenian predicates: late harvest, selection, berry selection, dried berry selection, ice wine
the pale, tart, low alcohol blend of red and white grapes of Dolenjska, a protected traditional name
Romanian and Moldovan for dry, off dry, medium sweet and sweet; alb is white, roșu red
Romanian for winery and for a vineyard region
Bulgarian for dry, red and white; izba is a winery
Czech for dry, off dry, medium sweet and sweet; bílé is white, červené red
Czech for ice wine and straw wine, the top rungs of the ripeness ladder
ladder: PDO and PGI, the six members of the European Union

The two European categories, protected designation of origin and protected geographical indication, each in local letters: Croatia ZOI and ZOZP, Slovenia ZGP and PGO, Romania DOC and IG, Bulgaria ZNP and ZGU, Czechia and Slovakia within a ripeness ladder of their own.
Croatia: vrhunsko, kvalitetno, stolno
Premium, quality and table wine, the older three tier scale that still appears on labels beneath ZOI, the PDO. Dingač on Pelješac was the first Croatian wine protected by law, in 1961.
Slovenia: ZGP, PGO and PTP
Vrhunsko vino ZGP is premium wine of protected origin, kakovostno vino ZGP quality wine, deželno vino PGO the regional PGI tier; PTP marks a recognised traditional name such as Cviček or Teran.
Georgia: appellation of origin

A register of appellations headed by the Kakheti names, Tsinandali, Mukuzani, Kindzmarauli, Napareuli, Akhasheni and Manavi, with Khvanchkara in Racha; each fixes grapes, zone and style, dry or naturally semi-sweet.
Romania: DOC with CMD, CT and CIB

Denumire de Origine Controlată is the PDO; its suffixes state ripeness at picking: CMD, picked at full maturity, CT, picked late, CIB, picked at the ennobling of the berries, that is botrytis. IG is the PGI.
Bulgaria: two PGI zones over the PDOs
The Danubian Plain north of the Balkan range and the Thracian Lowlands south of it are the two broad PGIs; the smaller PDO districts sit inside them.
Moldova: three PGI regions
Codru, Valul lui Traian and Ștefan Vodă are the protected geographical indications that most labels name; the National Office for Vine and Wine sits over the system.
Czechia and Slovakia: the ripeness ladder

Jakostní víno s přívlastkem in Czech, akostné víno s prívlastkom in Slovak: kabinet, late harvest (pozdní sběr, neskorý zber), selection of grapes, of berries, of raisined berries, ice wine and straw wine, on the Austrian and German pattern; VOC, started at Znojmo in 2009, is Czechia's origin based tier.
eastern-europe.overview:
The Certified exam treats these eight countries as one short chapter: a few grapes, places and dates each. Six belong to the European Union and print its two categories in local letters: Slovenia, Czechia and Slovakia since 2004, Romania and Bulgaria since 2007, Croatia since 2013. Georgia and Moldova sold mostly east until Russian embargoes from 2006 turned them towards Europe and America.

Georgia's story is the oldest. Residue in clay jars from villages south of Tbilisi, dated to about 6000 BC, is the earliest evidence of grape wine yet found, and the method survives: the qvevri, buried to its neck, where juice ferments with its skins, often its stems too, and rests through the winter. UNESCO listed the method in 2013. Kakheti in the east makes most of the wine, from red fleshed Saperavi and white Rkatsiteli.

The western edge belongs with Italy and Austria. Slovenia's Goriška Brda is Collio's hill country under another flag, with Rebula for Ribolla Gialla and the same taste for whites fermented on their skins. Croatia answers with Istrian Malvazija and Dalmatian Plavac Mali, the child of Tribidrag, the vine DNA matched to Zinfandel in 2001 under its other name, Crljenak Kaštelanski. Czechia and Slovakia grow Grüner Veltliner and Welschriesling on a Germanic ripeness ladder.

The east is the volume: Romania's Fetească family on both sides of the Carpathians, Bulgaria rebuilding on Mavrud after decades of bulk Cabernet, Moldova's cellars cut for kilometres into limestone. The exam leans on Georgia and Slovenia hardest, then on the grape synonyms that cross these borders.

places.name: Croatia
places.note: In the European Union since 2013, with ZOI and ZOZP for PDO and PGI, and the homeland of Tribidrag, which is Zinfandel.

places.name: Istria and Kvarner
places.note: The north western peninsula, terra rossa over limestone: dry Malvazija Istarska with its bitter almond finish, dark Teran, and Žlahtina on the island of Krk.

places.name: Dalmatia
places.note: The hot, stony southern coast and islands: Plavac Mali, Pošip and Grk on Korčula, Babić at Primošten, and Prošek from dried grapes.

places.name: Pelješac and Dingač
places.note: Dingač, a steep south facing slope on the Pelješac peninsula, became Croatia's first protected wine in 1961: Plavac Mali at full weight, with Postup next door.

places.name: Slavonia and the Danube
places.note: The continental east: Graševina, the local Welschriesling, at Kutjevo, Traminac at Ilok, and the oak sold as Slavonian.

places.name: Croatian Uplands
places.note: The cool hills around Zagreb, Zagorje and Plešivica: crisp whites, sparkling wine and light reds, closer to Slovenia than to the coast.

places.name: Slovenia
places.note: Three regions, named for the sea and two rivers: Primorska on the Adriatic side, Podravje on the Drava, Posavje on the Sava. Maribor keeps a Žametovka vine over four centuries old.

places.name: Primorska
places.note: The Adriatic side, sharing Friuli's climate: Goriška Brda, Vipava, Kras and Slovenian Istria, with Rebula, Malvazija, Refošk and Vipava's own Zelen and Pinela.

places.name: Goriška Brda
places.note: Collio continued across the border on the same flysch marl, opoka in Slovenian and ponca in Friulian: Rebula, Sauvignon and Merlot, and long skin maceration at houses such as Movia.

places.name: Kras
places.note: The limestone plateau above Trieste, whose iron red terra rossa grows Teran, a tart, dark Refošk under a protected traditional name.

places.name: Podravje
places.note: The north east, Štajerska and Prekmurje: Austria's Styria continued, with Laški rizling, Šipon, which is Furmint, Sauvignon and Riesling, mostly dry.

places.name: Posavje
places.note: The south east, Dolenjska, Bela krajina and Bizeljsko: home of Cviček, a pale, tart, low alcohol blend of red and white grapes.

places.name: Georgia
places.note: Over five hundred native grapes; buried qvevri give amber whites and dark reds, and naturally semi-sweet reds are a legal tradition, not a fault.

places.name: Kakheti
places.note: The east, along the Alazani valley around Telavi, with most of the vines and appellations: Tsinandali, dry white Rkatsiteli with Mtsvane; Mukuzani, dry Saperavi; Kindzmarauli and Akhasheni, naturally semi-sweet Saperavi. In the Kakhetian method the skins, and often the stems, stay in the qvevri for months.

places.name: Kartli
places.note: The centre around Gori and Mtskheta: Chinuri and Goruli Mtsvane, a sparkling tradition at Ateni, and a lighter, more European style.

places.name: Imereti
places.note: The humid west around Kutaisi: Tsolikouri, Tsitska and Krakhuna, fermented with only part of the skins, gentler than Kakheti.

places.name: Racha-Lechkhumi
places.note: The mountains north of Imereti, home of Khvanchkara, a naturally semi-sweet red of Aleksandrouli and Mujuretuli.

places.name: Romania
places.note: In the European Union since 2007: whites from Transylvania and the Moldavian hills, reds from the south, the Fetească family for identity, DOC and IG for law.

places.name: Dealu Mare
places.note: The big hill, south facing Carpathian foothills north of Bucharest: the most celebrated red district, with Fetească Neagră, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Cotnari
places.note: Near Iași in the north east: a historic sweet white led by Grasă de Cotnari with Fetească Albă, Frâncușă and Tămâioasă, botrytised in good years.

places.name: Transylvania and Târnave
places.note: The cool plateau inside the Carpathian arc: Fetească Regală, Fetească Albă, Traminer and Sauvignon, crisp whites and sparkling wine.

places.name: Murfatlar
places.note: In Dobrogea near the Black Sea at Constanța, among the sunniest districts: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and late harvest whites.

places.name: Drăgășani
places.note: On the Olt in Oltenia, with grapes of its own: white Crâmpoșie and the reds Negru de Drăgășani and Novac.

places.name: Bulgaria
places.note: Once the eastern bloc's bulk red supplier. The Balkan range splits it into two PGIs, the Danubian Plain north and the Thracian Lowlands south.

places.name: Thracian Lowlands
places.note: The warm Maritsa basin: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, Mavrud at Asenovgrad near Plovdiv, and Rubin, a Nebbiolo and Syrah cross of 1944.

places.name: Danubian Plain
places.note: The continental north: Cabernet, Merlot and Gamza, which is Kadarka; Pleven holds the national wine institute.

places.name: Struma Valley and Melnik
places.note: The hot south west towards Greece: Shiroka Melnishka Loza, the broad leaved Melnik vine, a late red of tobacco and dried fruit.

places.name: Moldova
places.note: Between Romania and Ukraine, with a very high share of its land under vine: three PGIs, vast cellars, and Rara Neagră and Fetească Neagră as native reds.

places.name: Codru
places.note: The forested centre around Chișinău, cooler than the south: white grapes lead, and the cellars of Cricova and Mileștii Mici run for kilometres through its limestone.

places.name: Valul lui Traian
places.note: The warm south west, named for Trajan's wall: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Saperavi and Rara Neagră.

places.name: Ștefan Vodă
places.note: The south east by the Dniester, where Purcari, founded in 1827, makes Negru de Purcari from Cabernet Sauvignon, Saperavi and Rara Neagră.

places.name: Czechia
places.note: Morava on the Austrian border holds nearly all the vines, Čechy near Prague the rest; VOC, an origin tier, began at Znojmo in 2009.

places.name: Morava
places.note: Znojmo, Mikulov, Velké Pavlovice and Slovácko: aromatic whites at Znojmo, Welschriesling and Pálava on Mikulov's limestone, reds at Velké Pavlovice.

places.name: Čechy
places.note: Small and cool on the Elbe around Mělník and Litoměřice, with Pinot Noir and Riesling at the edge of ripeness.

places.name: Slovakia
places.note: Six regions across the south, from the Small Carpathians to Slovak Tokaj: aromatic whites and Frankovka on an Austrian style ripeness ladder.

places.name: Small Carpathians
places.note: Malokarpatská, the slopes above Bratislava at Pezinok and Modra: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Riesling and Frankovka.

places.name: Slovak Tokaj
places.note: Seven villages across the Hungarian border, growing Furmint, Lipovina, which is Hárslevelű, and yellow Muscat for sweet wines under the shared name.

traps: Georgia's semi-sweet reds are naturally semi-sweet by law, the fermentation stopped by cold, not sweetened afterwards; Kindzmarauli is not a dessert wine.
Amber wine from a qvevri is a white wine made with its skins; it is not oxidised by definition, and the Imeretian style uses only a fraction of the skins.
Graševina, Laški rizling and Olaszrizling are Welschriesling, not Riesling, which Croatia labels Rajnski rizling and Slovenia Renski rizling.
Plavac Mali is Zinfandel's child, not Zinfandel: the parent is Tribidrag, also called Crljenak Kaštelanski.
Prošek is a Dalmatian sweet wine from dried grapes, still and sweet; it has nothing to do with Prosecco, whatever the fight over the name.

Teran is a protected Slovenian name on the Kras, yet a 2017 EU regulation lets Croatian Istria print it as a grape name in smaller type, and the EU General Court upheld that in September 2020; both are Refošk.
Moldova the country and Moldavia the Romanian region share a history and the Prut as a border; Cotnari is in Romania.
Tokaj is not only Hungarian: seven Slovak villages make it too under the shared name, and Furmint is the grape on both sides.

exam: The three sparkling grapes, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, and bottle fermentation with at least nine months on the lees under the PDO.
The south east: Kent, Sussex and Hampshire, and the chalk of the North and South Downs that continues under the Channel to Champagne.
The categories: English Wine PDO for vinifera, English Regional Wine PGI beneath it, and the Sussex PDO since 2022.
Bacchus as the still white to know, and Seyval Blanc as the hybrid of the early vineyard.
The climate: cool and maritime, high acidity, spring frost, wet flowering, and why that suits sparkling wine.
The dates: Merret's paper in 1662, Hambledon in 1952, Nyetimber in 1988.
English wine, from English grapes, against British wine, made from imported concentrate.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The backbone of English sparkling wine and of Blanc de Blancs, lean and citrus, and a still wine in warmer years.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Red fruit and body in sparkling blends and Blanc de Noirs, and a pale, delicate still red from warm sites.

grapes.name: Pinot Meunier
grapes.styles: The third Champagne grape, now usually called Meunier, ripening early and adding fruit and roundness to young blends.

grapes.name: Bacchus
grapes.styles: England's signature still white, a German crossing with elderflower, nettle and grapefruit, often compared with Sauvignon Blanc.

grapes.name: Seyval Blanc
grapes.styles: The French bred hybrid that carried the early English vineyard, crisp and neutral, still used for sparkling and still wine under the PGI.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: A small part of some sparkling blends and a soft still white.

grapes.name: Ortega
grapes.styles: An early ripening German crossing for aromatic still whites, often blended.

grapes.name: Reichensteiner
grapes.styles: Once widely planted, a neutral early crossing used in blends and sparkling bases.

grapes.name: Solaris
grapes.styles: A disease resistant variety of hybrid descent that ripens very early, rising on cool, damp sites.

grapes.name: Rondo
grapes.styles: A dark, early ripening red of hybrid descent, used for colour in blends and rosé.

from white grapes only, in England almost always Chardonnay
white wine from the black grapes, Pinot Noir and Meunier

ladder: English Wine PDO

The countrywide protected designation of origin, for still and sparkling wine from Vitis vinifera grown in England, with analysis and a tasting assessment; its quality sparkling wine is fermented in bottle and aged at least nine months on the lees.
Sussex PDO
Granted in 2022, the first county-scale English PDO: grapes from East or West Sussex, the traditional method for sparkling wine, and tighter rules than the countrywide name.
Darnibole PDO
A single vineyard PDO in Cornwall, granted in 2017, for still white wine from Bacchus.
English Regional Wine PGI
The protected geographical indication beneath the PDO, which admits hybrid grapes such as Seyval Blanc and suits blends and lighter styles.
Wine without a protected name
Wine from grapes grown in the United Kingdom outside the PDO and PGI, which may still state a variety and a vintage.
Welsh Wine PDO and Welsh Regional Wine PGI
Wales's own pair, on the same terms as England's.
British wine
Not English wine at all: a drink made in Britain from imported grape concentrate, outside every category above.
england.overview:
Vines came with the Romans, and the monasteries kept them until the Dissolution in the sixteenth century. After that England drank other people's wine: it became the great market for claret, port and sherry, and the place where strong, coal fired glass first made a wine under pressure safe to keep. In 1662 Christopher Merret read a paper to the Royal Society describing sugar added to finished wine to make it sparkle, the first written account of a deliberate second fermentation. The modern vineyard began in 1952 at Hambledon in Hampshire, and for forty years it leaned on German crossings and the hybrid Seyval Blanc, made into light, often off dry still whites.

The turn came in 1988, when Nyetimber in West Sussex planted only Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier for traditional method wine; its first releases in the 1990s won major awards. Ridgeview followed at Ditchling in 1995, Chapel Down grew at Tenterden in Kent, and a warming climate let the Champagne grapes ripen more often. Champagne houses themselves have since planted in Kent and Hampshire, and the national vineyard has grown many times over since 2000.

The climate is the whole argument. The North Atlantic Drift keeps winters mild for the latitude, but summers are cool, June flowering is often wet, spring frost is a constant danger and autumn rain can spoil a harvest, so yields swing widely from year to year. Grapes ripen slowly and keep searing acidity, a fault in many still wines and a virtue in a sparkling base that will spend years on its lees. The chalk of the North and South Downs is celebrated because it drains freely yet holds water in reserve, but many fine sites sit on greensand, sandstone or clay, so a county name does not promise chalk.

Since the United Kingdom left the European Union, its wine names have been protected under a British scheme that carried the old categories over in 2021. English Wine is the PDO for still and sparkling wine alike, from vinifera only, with analysis and tasting; its quality sparkling wine is fermented in bottle and rests at least nine months on its lees. English Regional Wine is the PGI, which admits hybrids. Two smaller PDOs sit inside: Darnibole in Cornwall, a single vineyard of Bacchus, from 2017, and Sussex, from 2022, the first drawn at county scale. Wales has its own matching pair. The exam leans on the PDO, the chalk, the three grapes, Bacchus, and the difference between English and British wine.

places.name: Kent
places.note: The North Downs chalk and the clays and greensand of the Weald, warm and sheltered in the south east: Chapel Down at Tenterden, Gusbourne at Appledore, and a Champagne house's own plantings. Sparkling wine first, with Bacchus and Pinot Noir for still wine.

places.name: Sussex
places.note: East and West Sussex, from the chalk of the South Downs to the greensand and clay of the Weald, with a PDO of its own since 2022. Nyetimber planted only the Champagne grapes here in 1988; Ridgeview at Ditchling, Wiston and Rathfinny are other names to know.

places.name: South Downs
places.note: The chalk ridge running east to west behind the coast, the same Cretaceous chalk as the Côte des Blancs, with Wiston and Rathfinny on its slopes and Ridgeview at its northern foot near Ditchling.

places.name: The Weald
places.note: The inland country between the North and South Downs, of sandstone, greensand and clay; Nyetimber's first vineyards at West Chiltington lie on greensand, not chalk.

places.name: Hampshire
places.note: Chalk downland west of Sussex, around Hambledon, where the modern English vineyard began in 1952; Hattingley Valley and Exton Park are names to know, and a Champagne house has planted here too.

places.name: Essex
places.note: The Crouch Valley's warm, dry, sheltered slopes on London clay, one of the sunniest corners of England, best known for still Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Bacchus and for fruit sold to sparkling houses elsewhere.

places.name: Surrey and the Thames Valley
places.note: North Downs chalk around Dorking, where Denbies farms a large single estate, and smaller vineyards west into Berkshire and the Chilterns.

places.name: Cornwall and the South West
places.note: Milder, wetter and windier: Camel Valley in Cornwall, whose Darnibole vineyard has its own PDO for Bacchus, and estates in Dorset and Devon.

places.name: Wales
places.note: Not England but sold beside it: a small, cool, wet vineyard in the south and along the border, with its own Welsh Wine PDO and Welsh Regional Wine PGI.

traps: British wine is made in Britain from imported grape concentrate; it is not English wine and carries no protected name.
Not every English sparkling vineyard is on chalk: much of the Weald is greensand and clay, and Nyetimber's first vineyards sit on greensand.
Hybrids such as Seyval Blanc are barred from the English Wine PDO and appear under the regional PGI.
Merret, after Christopher Merret, was floated as a generic name for English sparkling wine; it has no legal standing.
English sparkling wine may never be called Champagne, not even with style or method attached, whatever its grapes and chalk.
Sussex is a PDO inside the English one, not a replacement; Kent and Hampshire have no county PDO and use the countrywide names.
Welsh wine has its own PDO and PGI; it is not English wine.

exam: The Bekaa: altitude around a thousand metres, the two ranges that frame it, dry summers and snowmelt, and why the wines ripen without baking.
Château Musar: founded 1930, Cabernet Sauvignon with Cinsault and Carignan, made at Ghazir, released around seven years after harvest, and the civil war vintages.
The dates: Ksara 1857 and the Jesuits, Domaine des Tourelles 1868, Kefraya's first vintage 1979, Massaya 1998.
The native whites, Obaideh and Merwah, and the Rhône and Bordeaux reds the valley grows.
Arak: grape spirit with aniseed, distilled by many wineries, and how it is served with mezze.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: The Bekaa's historic red, planted for the French market and still in old vines: perfumed, soft and pale, a pillar of Musar's blend and of the valley's rosés.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The structural grape of the modern Bekaa red: cassis and cedar with ripe, dusty tannin, the lead at Kefraya and the backbone of Musar.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: The third grape of Musar and a frequent blender elsewhere, giving colour, acidity and a rustic grip to Cinsault's softness.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Widely planted since the 1990s: dark, spiced, Rhône in manner, often blended with Cabernet and Grenache at the newer estates.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: A southern French partner in the valley's blends and rosés, adding warmth and red fruit.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: A smaller part of the Rhône style blends of the Bekaa, bringing meaty depth.

grapes.name: Obaideh
grapes.styles: The native white of the mountains, sometimes likened to Chardonnay: full, nutty and long lived in Musar's oxidative white, and distilled for arak.

grapes.name: Merwah
grapes.styles: The second native white, sometimes likened to Sémillon, blended with Obaideh for Musar's white and used for arak.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The modern estates' white, often barrel fermented, round and ripe.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: A Rhône white that suits the valley's sun, apricot and blossom, often blended with Chardonnay or Sauvignon.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Fresh, herbal whites from the cooler sites and from Batroun, usually drunk young.

Bekaa Valley, Vallée de la Bekaa
the origin nearly every bottle states; spelt Beqaa on some labels
the national spirit: grape spirit redistilled with aniseed, served with water and ice, turning milky
the two native white grapes, the base of Musar's white and of much arak
Château Musar's second red, released younger and lighter than the grand vin
Château Musar's unoaked, early drinking range

ladder: Wine of Lebanon

There is no appellation ladder in force. Law 216 of 2000 defined wine and set standards; many wineries belong to the Union Vinicole du Liban, founded in 1997, and the National Institute of Vine and Wine that the law foresaw was approved in 2013.
Bekaa Valley on the label
A geographical statement rather than a controlled designation: it says where the grapes grew, and nearly all of them grow there.
The estates' own tiers
Houses rank their own wines: Musar's grand vin, then Hochar Père et Fils, then Musar Jeune; at Kefraya, Comte de M stands at the top.
lebanon.overview:
Wine has been made on this coast since the Phoenicians shipped it round the Mediterranean, and the Romans raised the Temple of Bacchus at Baalbek in the north of the Bekaa. Under Ottoman rule wine was tolerated for the Christian communities and little more, which is why the modern story begins with priests: Jesuits planted the Ksara vineyard in 1857 and later found Roman era caves beneath it that still serve as cellars. Domaine des Tourelles followed at Chtaura in 1868. The French mandate after 1920 brought a market and French habits, and Gaston Hochar founded Château Musar in 1930.

The civil war of 1975 to 1990 is the exam's human story. Musar went on picking and trucking grapes across the mountains through the fighting and failed to make wine in only two vintages; Château Kefraya made its first vintage in 1979, in the middle of it. Peace brought the modern estates, Massaya in 1998, Ixsir in 2008 and dozens more, and growers organised as the Union Vinicole du Liban in 1997, with a wine law passed in 2000 and a National Institute of Vine and Wine set up in 2013.

The geography is simple. The Bekaa is a high rift valley, not a lowland, running north to south between two parallel ranges; it is dry in summer, cold in winter, fed by winter snow and the Litani, and its altitude gives cool nights that hold acidity in grapes the sun ripens easily. Most vineyards lie in the west and centre of the valley, around Kefraya, Zahlé and Chtaura, with more vineyards to the north towards Baalbek. Newer districts have opened on the coastal mountains at Batroun in the north and at Jezzine in the south.

The grapes are French. Cinsault came first and remains the valley's old vine, then Cabernet Sauvignon, Carignan, Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre; among whites, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Viognier stand beside the two natives, Obaideh and Merwah, which Musar uses for its oxidative, long lived white. The exam leans on Musar, the Bekaa's altitude and ranges, the founding dates and arak.

places.name: Bekaa Valley
places.note: The heart of Lebanese wine: a high plateau around a thousand metres above the sea, between Mount Lebanon to the west and the Anti-Lebanon to the east, with the Litani river running down its length. Summers are dry and bright, winters snowy, and the altitude keeps nights cool enough for acidity. Nearly every house of note draws its grapes here, whether or not it makes the wine here.

places.name: West Bekaa
places.note: The southern and western side around Kefraya and Aana: Château Kefraya's vineyards on the slopes of Mount Barouk, and the vineyards Château Musar harvests before the grapes cross the mountains to Ghazir.

places.name: Zahlé and Chtaura
places.note: The central valley and its market towns: Château Ksara's cellars in the Roman caves near Zahlé, Domaine des Tourelles at Chtaura since 1868, and Massaya at Tanaïl.

places.name: Northern Bekaa and Baalbek
places.note: Hotter and drier towards Baalbek and its Temple of Bacchus, with vineyards around Deir el Ahmar.

places.name: Mount Lebanon
places.note: The coastal range above Beirut: Château Musar's winery and cellars at Ghazir, north of the capital, and a few mountain vineyards in the hills around Bhamdoun.

places.name: Batroun
places.note: Hills above the northern coast, where Ixsir, founded in 2008, and a cluster of smaller estates farm terraced slopes; a more maritime counterpart to the Bekaa.

places.name: Jezzine
places.note: A small pine clad district in the south above Sidon, high and cool, with a handful of estates.

traps: Musar's grapes grow in the Bekaa but the winery is at Ghazir on the coast north of Beirut, a mountain crossing away from the vines.
Musar's white is Obaideh and Merwah, not Chardonnay and Sémillon, whatever the resemblance claimed for them.
Cinsault is the Bekaa's old vine, in the valley before Cabernet Sauvignon arrived in quantity; it is not a minor filler.
The Bekaa's ripeness comes from sun and its freshness from altitude; it is a high plateau, not a lowland desert.
Lebanon has no appellation ladder: Bekaa Valley on the label is a geographical statement, and Château carries no legal weight.
Musar's red is deliberately released old and shows volatile lift and maturity as style; it is not a faulty bottle.

exam: The oldest winery of the Americas: Casa Madero, founded in 1597 at Parras in Coahuila.
The Valle de Guadalupe in Baja California, inland from Ensenada, the centre of the modern industry.
Latitude and its rescue: about thirty-two degrees north, made possible by the cold Pacific, fog and cool nights.
The Mission grape, Listán Prieto, carried north by missionaries into California.
Blends of many origins: Nebbiolo and Tempranillo with Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Syrah and Merlot.
The altitude regions, Coahuila and Querétaro, where height, not the sea, cools the nights.
Querétaro received protected wine geographical-indication status on 10 March 2025. Avoid the outdated blanket claim that Mexico has no protected wine origins.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.styles: Baja's emblematic red, warm, dark and firm, unlike Piedmont's; DNA work has questioned some of the vines planted under the name.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Ripe, round and spicy, alone or in blends, across Baja and the plateau.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The backbone of many blends in Baja and Coahuila, ripe and dark with firm tannin.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: Old vines in Baja give warm, red fruited wine and weight in blends.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The softening partner in Bordeaux style blends.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Dark and peppery reds and blends from Baja and Coahuila.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Old, dry farmed vines in Baja, rustic and fresh, revived as single variety wine.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.styles: Long planted in Baja, ripe and jammy, usually blended.

grapes.name: Petite Sirah
grapes.styles: Inky, tannic old vines in Baja, often blended.

grapes.name: Mission
grapes.styles: Listán Prieto, the Spanish grape the missionaries carried north, now rare but kept by a few producers.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Long a leading white in Baja and Coahuila, fresh and fruity, often off dry.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Crisp whites from the coolest Baja sites.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Rich still whites, and a base for Querétaro's sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Aromatic whites in Baja, often blended.

labels: sparkling wine, a speciality of Querétaro
a blend, the usual form of a Mexican red
the origin most bottles of note state, in Baja California
ladder: Protected geographical indications

Vinos de la Región Vitivinícola de Querétaro received geographical-indication protection on 10 March 2025. Check the applicable declaration and rules rather than assuming every regional name has identical protection.
Valley or state on the label

A valley or state name locates a wine, but its legal status must be checked individually. Querétaro now has a protected wine geographical indication; other names should not be assigned that status by analogy.
The producer's own ranges
Houses rank their own wines by name, and a cellar's top blend is marked by the producer rather than by law.
mexico.overview:
The history is long and interrupted. In 1524 Hernán Cortés ordered the settlers of New Spain to plant vines in proportion to the native labour they held, and vineyards spread so well that the Spanish crown, at the end of the sixteenth century, barred new planting to protect wine shipped from Spain. Missions kept vines for the sacrament, and from the end of the seventeenth century Jesuits, then Franciscans and Dominicans, carried them up the Baja California peninsula, the chain that brought the Mission grape into Alta California. At Parras, an oasis in the Coahuila desert named for its wild vines, the Hacienda de San Lorenzo began making wine in 1597; as Casa Madero it still does.

Brandy, not wine, carried most of the twentieth century, and table wine stayed a small trade until the 1980s. In Baja, Bodegas de Santo Tomás had opened at Ensenada in 1888, and Russian Molokan settlers farmed the Valle de Guadalupe from the early twentieth century. The large houses of the middle of the century were followed in the late 1980s by Monte Xanic, the first of the small estates, and after 2000 by a wave of boutique wineries, restaurants and hotels along the valley's wine route.

The Valle de Guadalupe lies inland from Ensenada, some fifty kilometres south of the United States border as the crow flies. On paper it is too hot: thirty-two degrees north is the latitude of North Africa. In fact the cold California Current sends fog and sea air through gaps in the hills each evening, and the nights are cool. Rain falls mostly in winter and is slight; groundwater is scarce and growing saline, which limits planting and makes old, dry farmed vines precious. The slopes are decomposed granite and sand, the valley floor alluvium and clay. On the central plateau, at 1,500 to 2,000 metres, altitude supplies the cool nights instead, but summer rain and hail near harvest are the risks.

Older guides described Mexican wine regions as geographic names without a controlled appellation framework. That blanket statement is now outdated: on 10 March 2025 Mexico protected Vinos de la Región Vitivinícola de Querétaro as a geographical indication. Read the particular designation and its requirements; a protected origin is not a national quality ranking. The exam asks the oldest winery and its date, the Valle de Guadalupe and the Pacific influence that makes it possible, the Mission grape's journey north, and the grapes of the modern blends.

places.name: Baja California
places.note: The peninsula south of the United States border that makes most of Mexico's wine, a Mediterranean climate saved by the cold Pacific: dry summers, slight winter rain, fog and sea breezes at night. Its wine valleys run inland from Ensenada and Tecate.

places.name: Valle de Guadalupe
places.note: The heart of Mexican wine, inland from Ensenada, with the old Russian settlement at Francisco Zarco and the villages of San Antonio de las Minas and El Porvenir: granite slopes, sandy alluvium, scarce and saline water, and blends of Nebbiolo, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache and Syrah. L.A. Cetto, Monte Xanic and Adobe Guadalupe are names a server meets.

places.name: Valle de Santo Tomás
places.note: South of Ensenada, the valley of the old Dominican mission that gave Bodegas de Santo Tomás, founded in 1888, its name, a valley open to Pacific air.

places.name: Valle de San Vicente
places.note: Further south along the peninsula, beyond Santo Tomás, another valley that sends fruit to the wineries around Ensenada.

places.name: Ojos Negros
places.note: A high inland valley east of Ensenada, colder at night, rising for whites and fresher reds.

places.name: Coahuila
places.note: The northern desert state where altitude, not the sea, cools the nights, and where the Americas' oldest winery still works.

places.name: Parras
places.note: An oasis of springs in the Coahuila desert at around 1,500 metres, its name meaning grapevines, where the Hacienda de San Lorenzo, now Casa Madero, began making wine in 1597.

places.name: Querétaro
places.note: A high plateau north of Mexico City, around Ezequiel Montes and Tequisquiapan, close to 2,000 metres, where summer rain favours early picked grapes and sparkling wine is the speciality, led by a large traditional method cellar founded by a Catalan cava house.

places.name: The central highlands
places.note: Aguascalientes, Zacatecas, Guanajuato around San Miguel de Allende, and San Luis Potosí: vineyards, many of them recent, high on the tropical plateau, betting on altitude for freshness.

places.name: Sonora and Chihuahua
places.note: The northern states where grapes are grown mostly for the table, for raisins and for brandy, with only a little wine.

traps: The oldest winery in the Americas is Mexican, at Parras in Coahuila, not in Peru or California.
Baja California is in Mexico; the shared name does not make it part of California or its AVA system.
Baja Nebbiolo is warm, dark and soft beside Barolo, and some vines carrying the name are not Nebbiolo at all.
Water, not heat, is the Valle de Guadalupe's hard limit: scarce and increasingly saline groundwater.
Querétaro's vineyards are among the highest in the country, and its best known wine is sparkling.
Mexican wine follows no single grape or style; a blend of Italian, Spanish and French grapes is normal.

exam: The six regions: the Valais largest, then Vaud, then Geneva, with the Three Lakes, Ticino and German speaking Switzerland after them.
Chasselas and its names: Fendant in the Valais, village names in Vaud, Gutedel in German speaking Switzerland.
Lavaux's terraces over Lake Geneva, listed by UNESCO in 2007, with Dézaley and Calamin its grand crus.
The Valais specialities, Petite Arvine, Amigne, Humagne Blanche, Humagne Rouge, Cornalin and Heida, and the synonyms Johannisberg, Ermitage and Malvoisie.
Reds: Pinot Noir the most planted grape, Dôle and Salvagnin as Pinot Noir and Gamay blends, Merlot in Ticino since 1906.
The law: AOC written canton by canton, with grand cru cantonal too.
Why the wines are rare abroad: small, steep, costly vineyards and a home market that drinks nearly everything.

grapes.name: Chasselas
grapes.styles: Neutral, soft and low in acid, made with full malolactic: lime blossom, pear and a stony, sometimes smoky finish that shows its site. Fendant in the Valais, village wines in Vaud, Dézaley at its peak.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The most planted grape in the country, from light Dôle blends to serious single variety reds in the Bündner Herrschaft, Neuchâtel and the Valais.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: Bright, fruity reds in Geneva and Vaud, and Pinot Noir's partner in Dôle and Salvagnin.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Ticino's grape since 1906, from supple everyday reds to oak aged wines of real depth, and a white pressed off the skins.

grapes.name: Petite Arvine
grapes.styles: The Valais's finest native white: saline, with grapefruit and rhubarb, bottled dry or sweet from shrivelled grapes; Fully is its best known home.

grapes.name: Cornalin
grapes.styles: A deep coloured, cherry and spice red of the Valais, also called Rouge du Pays, the offspring of two Aosta grapes.

grapes.name: Humagne Rouge
grapes.styles: A rustic, wild scented Valais red; it is the grape that Valle d'Aosta calls Cornalin.

grapes.name: Amigne
grapes.styles: A rare Valais white centred on Vétroz, often sweet, its sweetness shown by one to three bees on the label.

grapes.name: Heida
grapes.styles: Savagnin Blanc in the upper Valais, full and spicy, grown on the high terraces of Visperterminen.

grapes.name: Silvaner
grapes.styles: Sold as Johannisberg in the Valais, round and nutty, dry or sweet.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: A Valais speciality on warm slopes near Sion and Chamoson, peppery and fresh, the Rhône grape back near the Rhône's source.

grapes.name: Gamaret
grapes.styles: A Swiss crossing of Gamay with Reichensteiner, bred in 1970, deep coloured and rot resistant, blended in Geneva and Vaud.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: The mild, flowery white of German speaking Switzerland, usually labelled Riesling-Sylvaner, named after its Thurgau born breeder.

grapes.name: Marsanne
grapes.styles: Sold as Ermitage in the Valais, rich and often sweet.

ladder: AOC

Appellation d'origine contrôlée, defined by each canton within the federal wine ordinance: the canton or a smaller named area, the permitted grapes, maximum yields and minimum natural sugar. Most Swiss wine is AOC.
Grand Cru and Premier Grand Cru

Cantonal distinctions above AOC: in the Valais granted commune by commune with stricter yields and ripeness; in Vaud the grand cru appellations Dézaley and Calamin, and Premier Grand Cru for selected estates.
Vin de pays, Landwein
Country wine from a broader area, with looser rules than AOC.
Vin de table, Tafelwein
Plain Swiss wine with no origin narrower than the country.
switzerland.overview:
Swiss wine is a mountain viticulture of lakes and rivers. The vineyards ring the Alps: the upper Rhône through the Valais, the lakes of Geneva, Neuchâtel, Biel and Murten in the west, the valleys of Ticino south of the Alps, and the Rhine, Lake Zurich and the Bündner Herrschaft in the German speaking north and east. Six regions are named: the Valais, Vaud, Geneva, the Three Lakes, Ticino and German speaking Switzerland. Land is steep and dear, labour costly and yields modest, and the country exports only a tiny share of what it makes.

The climate is continental, tempered by water and wind. Lakes store warmth and throw light back onto the slopes; in Lavaux growers speak of three suns, the sky, the lake and the stone walls. The Valais lies in the rain shadow of high ranges on both sides and is among the driest places in the country, watered in places by old channels called bisses, and warmed in autumn by the foehn, a dry wind falling off the Alps. Terraces held by dry stone walls climb high; at Visperterminen vines grow above a thousand metres, among the highest in Europe.

Chasselas is thought to come from the Lake Geneva basin, and Switzerland is the country that takes it most seriously. It is neutral and low in acid, so Swiss growers usually let it complete malolactic fermentation and bottle it with a faint prickle and some lees character; it then speaks of its soil more clearly than of its fruit, and the best age well. Pinot Noir and Gamay make reds alone and together, as Dôle in the Valais and Salvagnin in Vaud. Merlot reached Ticino after phylloxera, in 1906. Switzerland's federal research station bred Gamaret and Garanoir, Gamay crossed with Reichensteiner, in 1970, and Müller-Thurgau carries the home canton of its Swiss born breeder in its name.

The federal wine ordinance sets three categories, AOC wine, country wine and table wine, but each canton writes its own AOC rules: boundaries, grapes, yields and minimum ripeness. Geneva adopted the first cantonal AOC, in 1988. Grand cru is cantonal too: the Valais grants it commune by commune, while Vaud has the grand cru appellations of Dézaley and Calamin and a Premier Grand Cru for selected estates. The exam asks the six regions, Chasselas and its names, the Valais natives, Lavaux and its UNESCO listing of 2007, and Ticino Merlot.

places.name: Valais
places.note: The largest wine canton, the upper Rhône valley from Visp down past Martigny: dry, sunny and foehn swept, on terraces of dry stone walls along the south facing right bank. Fendant, Pinot Noir and Gamay make the volume; Petite Arvine, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge, Amigne, Heida and Syrah are its treasures.

places.name: Sion and the central Valais
places.note: The heart of the canton around Sion, Sierre, Conthey and Chamoson: Fendant, Johannisberg, Syrah and Pinot Noir on steep, stony slopes and alluvial fans.

places.name: Fully and Vétroz
places.note: Fully's warm, steep slopes for Petite Arvine, and Vétroz, home of Amigne, whose labels show sweetness with one to three bees.

places.name: Visperterminen
places.note: Terraces in the German speaking upper Valais above a thousand metres, among the highest vineyards in Europe, for Heida, the local Savagnin.

places.name: Val d'Anniviers
places.note: The side valley above Sierre where vin du glacier is aged for years in larch casks topped up from one vintage to the next.

places.name: Vaud
places.note: The second canton, along the north shore of Lake Geneva and up towards Lake Neuchâtel: Chasselas country, labelled by village rather than grape, with Pinot Noir and Gamay for its reds.

places.name: Lavaux
places.note: Steep terraces between Lausanne and Montreux falling into the lake, listed by UNESCO in 2007 and warmed by the three suns of sky, lake and stone wall; Epesses, Saint-Saphorin and Lutry are among its villages.

places.name: Dézaley
places.note: Lavaux's grand cru on the steepest terraces facing south over the water, giving some of the richest and longest lived Chasselas in the country.

places.name: Calamin
places.note: Lavaux's second grand cru, a small enclave within the commune of Epesses, far less often seen than Dézaley.

places.name: Chablais
places.note: The valley where the Rhône runs into the lake, with Aigle and Yvorne giving flinty, firm Chasselas from scree and old rockfall.

places.name: La Côte
places.note: The gentle western shore between Lausanne and Geneva, the largest part of Vaud, with lighter Chasselas from Féchy, Mont-sur-Rolle and Morges.

places.name: Geneva
places.note: The third canton, in the countryside around the city on both banks of the Rhône; Satigny in the Mandement is the largest wine commune in the country. Gamay leads the reds with Gamaret and Garanoir, and Chasselas, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir follow.

places.name: Three Lakes
places.note: The lakes of Neuchâtel, Biel and Murten at the foot of the Jura, on limestone: Chasselas, released unfiltered each January in Neuchâtel, Pinot Noir and Oeil de Perdrix, the pale rosé the canton made its own.

places.name: Ticino
places.note: The Italian speaking south of the Alps, sunny but wet, where Merlot arrived after phylloxera in 1906 and now dominates, as red, rosé and even white; Monte Ceneri divides the Sopraceneri to the north from the Sottoceneri to the south.

places.name: German speaking Switzerland
places.note: The north and east, from Basel to Lake Constance: Pinot Noir as Blauburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, and Räuschling around Lake Zurich, with Schaffhausen, Zurich and Aargau among its main cantons.

places.name: Bündner Herrschaft
places.note: Four villages of Graubünden on the Rhine, Fläsch, Maienfeld, Jenins and Malans, where the foehn ripens some of the country's most admired Pinot Noir and the old white Completer survives.

traps: Fendant is not a separate grape; it is the Valais name for Chasselas.
The Valais's Cornalin, Rouge du Pays, is not Aosta's Cornalin: the Aosta grape of that name is the Valais's Humagne Rouge.
Humagne Blanche and Humagne Rouge are unrelated grapes despite the shared name.
Johannisberg in the Valais is Silvaner, not Riesling, and Swiss Riesling-Sylvaner is Müller-Thurgau.
Malolactic fermentation is normal for Swiss Chasselas; a soft, low acid white is the style here, not a fault.
Vaud labels name the village, Epesses, Dézaley or Yvorne, without saying Chasselas; the grape is implied.
Swiss Merlot comes from Ticino, the Italian speaking south, not from the French speaking west.

exam: Tannat: Madiran's grape, brought by Pascual Harriague to Salto in the 1870s, called Harriague for decades, now the national red.
Canelones holds most of the vines, around Montevideo on clay over limestone; Maldonado on the Atlantic is the new coastal face on granite.
Humidity as the central problem: rain through the growing season, rot, the lyre trellis and open canopies, hand harvest in February to April.
INAVI since 1987, VCP against VC, and departments as the regional names.
The partners that soften Tannat: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo, Marselan, and micro-oxygenation; Albariño as the rising white.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.styles: The national red: deep colour, blackberry and plum, firm but rounder tannin than Madiran's thanks to the humid climate, micro-oxygenation and oak, made as a varietal, a blend, a rosé and even a sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The classic softening partner to Tannat in the Canelones blends.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Blended with Tannat and increasingly bottled alone: fresh, herbal and red fruited in the maritime climate.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: A Spanish import blended with Tannat at Bouza and others to temper the tannin.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Planted widely in the replanting years; firm reds in the warmer north and in blends.

grapes.name: Marselan
grapes.styles: A Cabernet Sauvignon and Grenache cross that ripens evenly in the humidity, planted for varietal reds and blends.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: The white that suits the Atlantic: saline, citric and peachy in Maldonado, leaner in Canelones, the country's most convincing white.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Crisp, grassy whites from the coast, usually drunk young.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: For still whites and the traditional method sparkling wines of the family houses.

Vino de Calidad Preferente, the quality category, the one a server will meet
national drink: a decree of 2014 declared Uruguayan wine the national drink, and the words appear on its labels
a winery; viñedo is a vineyard

ladder: VCP, Vino de Calidad Preferente
Wine of preferred quality: from Vitis vinifera, bottled in 750 millilitres or less, with its label registered at INAVI before release. Nearly every bottle a server will meet belongs here.
VC, Vino Común
Common wine for the home market, sold in larger containers; the bulk of what the country drank for most of its history.
The department
Uruguay's nineteen departments stand in for regions on the label: Canelones, Montevideo, Maldonado, Colonia, San José, Rivera, Salto and Paysandú are the ones that matter.
INAVI
The Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura, founded in 1987, which registers vineyards and labels, runs the categories and promotes the country's wine.
uruguay.overview:
Uruguay sits between Brazil and Argentina with the Río de la Plata along its south and the Atlantic along its east, a rolling country of grassland whose highest point barely passes five hundred metres. There are no Andes here and no desert: rain falls through the growing season, humidity is high, and the sea moderates everything. That is the whole key to the style. Tannat, the most tannic grape of south west France, ripens with rounder tannin and fresher fruit than in Madiran, and the growers' craft lies in keeping bunches dry.

The vine came with the colonists, but the modern industry dates from the 1870s, when Pascual Harriague, a Basque settler at Salto in the north west, planted Tannat from south west France, and Francisco Vidiella planted Folle Noire at Colón, on the edge of Montevideo. Both vines carried their planters' names for decades. Italian, Spanish and Basque families then filled Canelones, just north of Montevideo, with small mixed farms, and the country drank its own common wine for a century.

The turn to quality came after 1987, when INAVI, the national vine and wine institute, was founded by law and led a replanting of the vineyard with better clones and vinifera varieties, and the two categories VCP and VC were set: wine of preferred quality in bottles of 750 millilitres or less, and common wine in larger containers. Family houses in Canelones and Montevideo, Juanicó, Pisano and Bouza among them, built the reputation of Tannat abroad; Carrau planted Cerro Chapeu on the sandy Brazilian border at Rivera; and from the 2000s Maldonado's granite hills near Punta del Este drew large investment, Bodega Garzón above all, with Albariño beside Tannat.

On the label a department is the regional name: Canelones, Montevideo, Maldonado, Colonia, San José, Rivera, Salto, Paysandú. Tannat is made as a varietal, often with micro-oxygenation and oak, and as a blend with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo or Marselan to soften it. The exam leans on Tannat and Madiran, Harriague and the 1870s, Canelones against Maldonado, humidity and the lyre.

places.name: Canelones
places.note: The department beside Montevideo, to its north and east, holding most of the country's vineyards on clay and clay over limestone within reach of the Río de la Plata: the heartland of Tannat and of the immigrant family wineries that built the industry.

places.name: Juanicó and Las Violetas
places.note: The wine villages north of the capital where the largest family houses stand, Juanicó's estate among them, with Tannat, Merlot and sparkling wine.

places.name: Progreso
places.note: A Canelones town of small estates, Pisano's among them, where Tannat is made in a ripe, generous style and blended with Merlot or Cabernet Franc.

places.name: Montevideo
places.note: The capital's own department, with vineyards at Melilla on its northern edge, where Bouza farms Tannat, Albariño and Tempranillo on clay loam minutes from the city.

places.name: Maldonado
places.note: The Atlantic department around Punta del Este, planted on decomposed granite hills a short way from the ocean: firm, fresh Tannat, saline Albariño and the country's largest modern investment at Garzón.

places.name: Garzón
places.note: The hill village inland from José Ignacio where Bodega Garzón opened its winery in 2016, with many small granite parcels of Tannat and Albariño open to the Atlantic breeze.

places.name: Colonia
places.note: The south western department across the river from Buenos Aires, with old estates around Carmelo and some of the country's oldest cellars; Tannat and Cabernet.

places.name: San José
places.note: West of Canelones, a smaller department of family estates on similar clay soils, part of the same Río de la Plata belt.

places.name: Rivera
places.note: The northern border with Brazil, hotter and inland, where Carrau's Cerro Chapeu vineyard stands on deep sandy soils; Tannat and Cabernet with a riper, drier profile than the coast.

places.name: Salto
places.note: In the north west on the Río Uruguay, warm and far from the coast, where Pascual Harriague planted Tannat in the 1870s: the history of the national grape begins here.

places.name: Paysandú
places.note: South of Salto on the Río Uruguay, warm and continental, with a few estates and early harvests.

traps: Uruguay is low, rolling and maritime; it has no Andes and no desert, so do not import Mendoza's altitude story.
Tannat is softer in Uruguay than in Madiran because of climate and handling, not because the grape is different.
Canelones, not Maldonado, is the largest wine department; Maldonado is the newer coastal showcase.
Harriague is a name for Tannat, not a separate grape, and Vidiella was the name for Folle Noire.
Uruguayan Albariño is the Galician grape, planted near the Atlantic as at home, not a local synonym for something else.
Uruguay has no appellation ladder of the European kind: VCP and VC are quality categories, and the department is the regional name.
